query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In steels for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, an optimal level of silicon (~1.3 wt.%) synergistically combined with a controlled, moderately refined (as opposed to ultrafine) grain structure promotes the rapid in situ formation of a continuous, dual-layer protective oxide film (with an inner Cr-/Si-enriched phase and an outer iron-rich phase) that inhibits both oxidation and dissolution. This oxide film limits oxygen ingress and element leaching even under high-temperature, oxygen-controlled, and liquid-metal conditions, whereas excessive grain refinement (ultrafine) may instead enhance dissolution by providing too many reactive grain-boundary sites.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline ferritic–martensitic steel similar to T91 containing standard Cr and low Si, with conventional (coarse to moderately refined) grain size.
generation.intervention: Prepare modified steel samples with identical base composition but with controlled silicon additions (targeting ~1.3 wt.%) and two distinct grain structures produced via tailored thermomechanical processing: one with moderate grain refinement (fine grains) and one with ultrafine grains.
generation.conditions: Expose samples to (a) an aqueous chloride environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl at ~25–50 °C, representative of chemical processing conditions) and (b) a high-temperature liquid-metal environment (e.g., liquid Pb or lead–bismuth eutectic at 550–600 °C with controlled oxygen levels around 10−6 wt.%) for extended durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a stable, continuous dual-layer oxide film—comprising an inner Cr-/Si-rich barrier that slows oxygen diffusion and an outer iron-rich (or mixed Fe/lead oxide) layer that protects the substrate.
generation.mechanism: Silicon’s strong oxygen affinity lowers the Gibbs energy for forming a protective oxide (e.g., SiOx or mixed Cr-Si oxides) and, when combined with a moderate density of grain boundaries, accelerates the nucleation and lateral growth of a continuous passive film. However, if the structure is too ultrafine, the high density of reactive grain boundaries may increase the rate of component dissolution (as seen in some ODS steels), thereby offsetting any benefit from rapid film formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline steel, samples with ~1.3 wt.% Si and moderate grain refinement will exhibit a significantly lower corrosion rate (e.g., a reduction in corrosion penetration depth by around 40% under liquid-metal exposure) and display a more uniform and adherent dual-layer oxide film, whereas ultrafine-grained variants may show increased element dissolution and less effective film continuity under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: Steel with no additional Si (or too low Si content) and with standard or ultrafine grain size, expected to form discontinuous or less protective oxide films, leading to higher corrosion rates and deeper corrosive penetration.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for steels operating in environments typical of chemical process equipment (aqueous chloride systems) and nuclear reactor components (high-temperature liquid-metal conditions) under controlled oxygen concentrations. Deviations in temperature, oxygen partial pressure, or alloying elements beyond the tested ranges may lead to altered behavior.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the findings from PMC9028533 (Si addition promoting a thinner, stable oxide with an inner Si-rich layer) and PMC6702197 (grain size effects on passive film quality in AISI 321) along with the observation in PMC10054900 that ultrafine grains in 9Cr ODS can lead to accelerated dissolution. What is new is the targeted combination of optimized Si content with a tunable grain structure evaluated side by side in both corrosive aqueous and liquid-metal environments. Uncertainties remain regarding the exact balance point between beneficial film formation and detrimental grain-boundary reactivity, especially under high-temperature liquid-metal conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of steel samples with identical base composition varying only in Si content (including 0 wt.%, ~1.3 wt.%, and higher than 1.3 wt.%) and in controlled grain sizes (moderate vs. ultrafine). Subject these samples concurrently to two test environments – an aqueous chloride solution (3.5 wt.% NaCl at 25–50 °C) and a high-temperature liquid Pb/LBE corrosion test at 550–600 °C with controlled oxygen levels. Use in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and post-exposure microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS, TEM) to assess oxide film structure, continuity, and corrosion penetration.
measurements: Corrosion rate (via weight loss and pit depth measurement)
Surface oxide film continuity, thickness, and composition (via SEM/EDS and TEM)
Electrochemical impedance spectra to determine film resistance and charge transfer resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with ~1.3 wt.% Si and moderate grain refinement do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance (e.g., no reduction in corrosion rate or film discontinuities similar to the baseline) in either the aqueous or liquid-metal tests – or if ultrafine-grained samples unexpectedly perform better – then the hypothesized synergistic mechanism between Si addition and controlled grain size is not supported.

AbstractThe role of grain size and strain rate on the corrosion behavior of plastically-deformed Ti-stabilized austenitic stainless steel (AISI 321) in saline media was investigated. The as-received coarse-grained alloy (CG: ~37 µm) was subjected to thermomechanical processing to develop fine (FG: ~3 µm) and ultrafine (UFG: ~0.24 µm) grained structures. These samples were deformed under high (dynamic) and low (quasi-static) strain-rate conditions to a similar true strain of ~0.86. Microstructural analyses on specimens after deformation prior to corrosion study suggests a shift from the estimated stacking fault energy value of the steel. Electrochemical tests confirm the highest corrosion resistance for UFG specimens due to the formation of the most stable adsorbed passive film. This is followed by FG and CG specimens in that order. For the three grain sizes, the corrosion resistance of specimen deformed under quasi-static loading condition is higher than that subjected to dynamic impact loading while the corrosion resistance of undeformed samples is the least. AbstractThe 9–12% Cr ferritic–martensitic heat-resistant steel is the main candidate structural material for the Lead-cooled Faster Reactor. The lower Gibbs free energy change of Si oxide can promote the formation of a stable oxide layer, which can improve the corrosion resistance of the material. Therefore, it is of great significance to study the effect of silicon (Si) on the corrosion resistance of T91 steel in lead–bismuth eutectic (LBE). The corrosion resistance of T91 steel with Si contents of 0.5 wt.%, 1.3 wt.%, and 2.0 wt.%, both in dynamic and static LBE at 550 °C, was investigated. The microstructure was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscope (SEM) and transmission electron microscope (TEM), while the oxide films were characterized by electron probe microanalysis (EPMA). Results show that the addition of Si is conducive to improving the corrosion resistance of T91 steel in LBE. T91 steel with high Si content has a thinner and more stable oxide film. The change of Si content can change the contact angle between the steel and LBE, and the contact angle is the largest when the Si content is 1.3 wt.%. The corrosion failure modes of materials in LBE are oxidation and dissolution, and the root cause is diffusion. On the one hand, the matrix material diffuses into LBE, on the other hand, oxygen diffuses into the matrix. The corrosion mechanism and oxide film behavior of 9–12% Cr steel in LBR were studied, and a more classical oxide film growth model was put forward []. In this study, the change of oxide film after the addition of Si is studied, the formation sequence of oxide film in different layers is analyzed from the perspective of the formation energy of various oxides, and a new model is proposed. Excessively high oxygen content in LBE will produce a thick oxide film which can protect the material from further corrosion, but the falling off of the oxide film is easy to block the flow channel, thus affecting the reactor operation. It is hard to form a continuous oxide film in the oxygen-depleted LBE solution, so that the matrix cannot be protected from corrosion. Therefore, the ideal oxygen content in the alloy is of great significance for improving the corrosion resistance of structural materials in LBE. However, excessive N will produce a Cr-rich nitride zone in stainless steel, and the Cr content in the stainless steel will be significantly reduced, preventing the stainless steel from forming a passive film on the surface, which destroys its corrosion resistance. To solve this problem, Zhang and Bell invented the low-temperature plasma nitriding process, which not only improves the wear resistance but also maintains the corrosion resistance of stainless steel []. It is found that austenitic stainless steel can produce supersaturated nitrogen-containing austenite after low-temperature plasma nitriding, causing lattice distortion of austenite and producing the wear- and corrosion-resistant S phase [,,]. The elemental N of the S phase is dissolved in the austenite, which inhibits the precipitation of CrN at the grain boundary and improves the wear resistance to ensure corrosion resistance.
